title: NPS for NRIs: What Happens to Your Retirement Account When You Move Abroad
excerpt: PFRDA allows NRIs to continue their NPS Tier I accounts through NRE or NRO bank accounts, but Tier II is off-limits — and renouncing citizenship triggers separate closure rules.
body:
• NRIs and Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) can continue holding an NPS Tier I account after moving abroad — the account is not automatically closed.
  • NRI subscribers must link their NPS account to an NRE or NRO bank account as part of the documentation requirements.
  • Tier II accounts cannot be activated by NRI or OCI subscribers, per PFRDA guidelines since 2019.
  • Indians who renounce citizenship without holding an OCI card face separate account closure and corpus settlement rules under an April 2025 PFRDA circular.

Your NPS Account Doesn't Close Automatically

One of the most common questions Indians face when relocating abroad is what happens to their National Pension System savings. The answer, according to the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, is straightforward: moving abroad does not require exiting NPS. The pension regulator describes NPS as portable across employment and geographic locations.

NRIs and OCIs can subscribe to and continue holding an NPS Tier I account. For NRI subscribers, PFRDA requires proof of an NRE or NRO bank account as part of the documentation. The same requirement applies to OCIs. Contributions continue through the available contribution channels, invested according to the pension fund and asset allocation selected by the subscriber.

The Tier II Restriction

There is an important distinction between NPS Tier I and Tier II for non-residents. PFRDA explicitly states that NRIs and OCIs with Tier I accounts are not permitted to activate a Tier II account. The regulator's FAQ lists NRIs and OCIs as ineligible for Tier II. This restriction has been in place since at least 2019, when PFRDA clarified the position while permitting OCIs to enroll in NPS.

For someone moving abroad who already has both Tier I and Tier II accounts, the transition requires careful planning. The Tier II restriction means the same flexibility available to resident subscribers will not carry over after becoming an NRI.

Investment Options Remain Flexible

NRI subscribers retain access to the same investment framework as resident subscribers within Tier I. Under Active Choice, subscribers decide how their money is allocated among equity, corporate bonds, and government securities. Equity allocation can go up to 75% under common schemes, while corporate bonds and government securities can each reach up to 100%, subject to overall allocation limits.

Subscribers can also use Auto Choice, where allocation across asset classes is determined by a life-cycle strategy based on the subscriber's age. PFRDA allows subscribers to change their pension fund once per financial year and their investment choice four times per financial year.

What If You Renounce Citizenship

The rules change significantly for NPS subscribers who renounce Indian citizenship and do not hold an OCI card. PFRDA issued a separate circular in April 2025 covering the closure of such NPS accounts and settlement of the accumulated corpus. This is a distinct situation from simply becoming an NRI, which allows continued participation.

Practical Steps for Indians Moving Abroad

For Indians relocating overseas while retaining citizenship, the key steps are: link the NPS account to an NRE or NRO bank account, understand that Tier II will not be available going forward, and review asset allocation choices given the changed tax and currency environment. The NPS corpus does not need to be withdrawn, and the account remains active as long as the banking and documentation requirements for non-residents are met.

PFRDA's framework ensures that moving abroad is not a forced exit from India's pension system — but the restrictions on Tier II and the separate rules for citizenship renunciation mean that non-residents face a narrower set of options than their counterparts still living in India.
